strengths: The work addresses a valuable computer-vision application: reusable representations of irregular optical and radar time series. Compact, annual 128-dimensional embeddings could substantially simplify downstream Earth-observation workflows.

The strongest controlled comparison is canopy-height estimation: with the same downstream architecture and training procedure, TESSERA achieves RMSE 8.88 m versus PRESTO’s 10.73 m and R² 0.66 versus 0.50 (Fig. 3). Spatial holdouts and repeated training runs strengthen this evidence.

Crop classification shows consistent improvements over PRESTO with identical MLP heads, including limited-label settings. BioMassters provides additional evidence of useful transfer: TESSERA with 1% of training labels outperforms the reported SpectralGPT result using all labels, although their pipelines differ.

Pretraining on approximately 0.8 billion samples is a substantial engineering effort. The manuscript supplies useful details about temporal sampling, optimization, computational cost, and global data shuffling.
weaknesses: The methodological contribution is insufficiently isolated. Temporal Barlow Twins learning builds explicitly on [49], and mix-up follows [9]. There are no downstream ablations establishing the benefits of sensor fusion, temporal encoding, mix-up, projector size, or pretraining scale. Figure 8 demonstrates smoother training loss with global shuffling, but does not establish improved transfer or geographic generalization.

The crop evaluation does not specify whether train, validation, and test sets are separated by agricultural parcel or geographic block (Appendix B.2). Random pixel subsets can share strongly correlated observations from the same fields, so the reported results do not establish transfer to unseen parcels or regions. Patch overlap and spatial separation are also insufficiently documented.

Several comparisons confound representation quality with other factors. Crop segmentation uses UNet for pixel-based models and UPerNet for patch-based models; biomass comparisons also differ in decoder and satellite inputs. Locally supervised canopy models are compared against fixed global products without equivalent local adaptation. These are useful pipeline comparisons, but cannot support the broad claim of uniformly superior representations.

Two of the five applications provide substantially weaker evidence. Burned-area analysis consists of UMAP visualizations from two regions, without detection metrics or baselines; event separation could also reflect geographic or vegetation differences. For the 38-site carbon-market experiment, the TESSERA-to-GEDI structural prediction procedure is not adequately described, and no independent evaluation of the fitted biomass calibration is reported.

Important implementation details conflict or are missing. Figure 1 specifies GRU pooling, whereas Sections 1.1 and A.5 specify attention pooling. Temporal encoding is described both as learned additive positional encoding and concatenated sinusoidal features. The quantization operation and its training treatment are unspecified, and 'spatially downsampled by a factor of 400' does not distinguish subsampling from spatial aggregation. These ambiguities materially obstruct reproduction.

The global data product is central to the contribution, but Appendix A.8.2 describes code, weights, and maps as intended releases and supplies no access mechanism or coverage accounting. Its practical availability cannot therefore be credited as demonstrated. Overall, the encouraging transfer results are outweighed by unresolved evaluation and reproducibility concerns; the issue is not failure to beat the task-specific BioMassters winner.

strengths: The problem is important, and annual 128-dimensional representations combining optical and SAR time series offer a useful interface for downstream Earth observation. Precomputed features could substantially reduce users’ data-processing and inference burden.

The canopy-height experiment provides meaningful evidence: spatial cross-validation and repeated training runs yield R² = 0.66 and RMSE = 8.88 m, compared with PRESTO’s R² = 0.50 and RMSE = 10.73 m using the same downstream architecture and training procedure (Figure 3).

Crop classification shows consistent improvements over PRESTO and Random Forest across label budgets, including few-shot settings. The identical MLP heads used for TESSERA and PRESTO make this a useful representation comparison.

The BioMassters evaluation uses a substantial fixed test set of 2,773 patches and demonstrates promising label efficiency. The manuscript appropriately acknowledges that the task-specific competition winner remains better.
The supplement documents substantial implementation details, including temporal sampling, training scale, optimizer settings, computational cost, and geographic shuffling.
weaknesses: The methodological contribution is insufficiently isolated. Temporal Barlow Twins learning explicitly builds on prior work [49], and mix-up follows [9]. There are no downstream ablations separating the benefits of sensor fusion, temporal information, mix-up, projector size, or pretraining scale. Figure 8 demonstrates smoother training loss with global shuffling, but does not establish improved transfer or geographic generalization. Consequently, the reasons for the reported gains remain unclear.

The crop evaluation does not specify whether training, validation, and test samples are separated by agricultural parcel or geographic region (Appendix B). Randomly selected pixel subsets could share highly correlated fields across splits; patch overlap is also unspecified. This does not establish leakage, but leaves a consequential uncertainty in the principal classification evidence and its few-shot interpretation.

Several comparisons do not isolate representation quality. Crop segmentation uses UNet for pixel-based models and UPerNet for other models; BioMassters likewise compares TESSERA+UNet against SpectralGPT+UPerNet with differing satellite inputs. Locally supervised canopy predictions are compared with existing global products lacking equivalent local supervision. These comparisons demonstrate practical pipeline performance, but support a narrower conclusion than general superiority over competing foundation models.

Wildfire detection is supported only by UMAP visualizations from two regions, without held-out detection metrics or baseline comparisons. Spatially distinct fires can separate because of location or vegetation differences, so the plots alone do not establish sensitivity to fire timing or severity. This task does not substantiate the abstract’s claim of benchmarked superiority across five tasks.

The carbon-market experiment lacks the essential mapping from TESSERA embeddings to the GEDI RH90–RH10 quantity described in Figure 6. Training data, model specification, and independent evaluation are not documented. Linear calibration minimizes error against the 38 field sites, but no held-out calibration protocol is reported. The referenced supplementary details are absent from the supplied appendices, making this result difficult to assess or reproduce.

Implementation descriptions conflict: Figure 1 specifies GRU pooling whereas Sections 1.1 and A.5 specify attention pooling; temporal encoding is described as both learned additive encoding and concatenated sine/cosine features; Figure 2’s caption specifies UPerNet for TESSERA while Appendix B specifies UNet. Quantization is introduced without its implementation or gradient treatment. These affect reconstruction of the actual model, beyond presentation polish.

The global data product is a potentially substantial contribution, but Appendix A.8.2 describes public release as intended, while the main text presents accessibility as established. The manuscript supplies no access mechanism, coverage audit, storage footprint, or global inference cost. Taken together with the evaluation and reproducibility uncertainties, this leaves the supported contribution promising but insufficient for acceptance.

strengths: TESSERA addresses a valuable problem: learning reusable, annual, 10 m representations from irregular optical and SAR observations. Compact, precomputed embeddings could substantially simplify downstream Earth observation workflows.

The canopy-height experiment provides meaningful evidence through spatial cross-validation and repeated training runs. With comparable downstream models, TESSERA achieves RMSE 8.88 m and R² 0.66 versus PRESTO’s 10.73 m and 0.50 (Fig. 3).

The crop experiments show consistent improvements over PRESTO and traditional baselines across label budgets, including few-shot settings. BioMassters also demonstrates useful transfer: TESSERA with 1% of training labels outperforms the reported full-data SpectralGPT baseline, although the task-specific competition winner remains better.

The engineering effort is substantial: pretraining uses approximately 0.8 billion samples from 3,012 tiles. The appendix reports training hardware, optimization settings, temporal sampling, and the global shuffling pipeline, providing useful implementation information.
weaknesses: The crop evaluation does not establish field-level or spatial independence between training and testing. Appendix B describes random subsets and held-out sets without specifying parcel separation, spatial buffers, or patch overlap restrictions. Spatial autocorrelation could materially affect the reported label efficiency; leakage is not demonstrated, but the protocol is insufficiently specified to rule it out.

Several comparisons cannot isolate representation quality. BioMassters compares different decoders and satellite inputs, while canopy-height comparisons pit a locally supervised TESSERA model against externally trained map products. These are useful practical comparisons, but support narrower conclusions than general superiority over competing methods. The matched PRESTO canopy comparison is more persuasive.

Two of the five advertised tasks lack convincing predictive evaluation. Burned-area results consist of UMAP visualizations from two regions, without held-out detection or severity metrics; geographic and vegetation differences could also explain separation between fires. For the 38-site carbon-market experiment, the connection between TESSERA embeddings and the GEDI-derived index is insufficiently explained, and independent evaluation of the fitted calibration is not established.

The method builds on prior temporal Barlow Twins representations, standard Transformer encoders, and an existing mix-up objective. There are no downstream ablations isolating temporal sampling, sensor fusion, mix-up, or pretraining scale. Figure 8 shows smoother training loss with global shuffling, but does not establish improved transfer. Consequently, the source of the empirical gains and the methodological contribution remain unclear.

Reproduction is hindered by conflicting descriptions of core components: attention pooling versus GRU pooling, learned additive temporal encodings versus concatenated sine/cosine features, and UPerNet versus UNet for crop segmentation. Quantization is introduced without implementation details, and spatial downsampling by a factor of 400 is ambiguous. These affect the actual model and experiments, beyond presentation polish.

The central resource contribution is not adequately substantiated in the supplied manuscript. Global 2017–2024 maps and open-source access are presented as accomplishments, while Appendix A.8.2 describes release as intended and supplies no access mechanism or coverage audit. Overall, the quantitative results are worthwhile, but unresolved evaluation protocols, incomplete task evidence, and implementation ambiguities currently outweigh the case for acceptance.

strengths: TESSERA makes a valuable contribution to practical geospatial representation learning: a globally trained optical–SAR temporal encoder producing compact, precomputed 10 m embeddings. The reported release of model weights, processing code, embeddings, and retrieval tools substantially reduces the expertise and computation required for downstream applications. This systems and resource contribution supports acceptance despite limited algorithmic novelty.

The canopy-height experiment provides convincing evidence of representation quality. With matched UNet heads, spatially held-out evaluation, and three runs across each of four spatial splits, TESSERA achieves RMSE 8.88 ± 0.98 m, compared with 10.73 m for PRESTO, 11.83 m for GSE, and 10.66 m for Sentinel-2 composites (Fig. 3). These controlled comparisons are more informative than comparisons against unadapted global products.

The crop and biomass experiments demonstrate useful transfer and label efficiency. Crop classification compares identical MLP heads across TESSERA, PRESTO, and GSE, including few-shot settings. On BioMassters, evaluation uses 2,773 fixed test patches and five random training splits; TESSERA with 1% of training labels outperforms the evaluated SpectralGPT pipeline using all labels (Fig. 4).

The ablations provide actionable evidence for design choices. Removing global shuffling or mixup reduces crop validation F1 from 0.773 to 0.681 or 0.662, respectively, while removing quantization improves it only to 0.779 (Table 4). This supports the practicality of compact embeddings and the importance of geographically diverse training batches.
weaknesses: The crop evaluation does not establish spatial generalization. Appendix E describes randomly selected training subsets and held-out validation/test data without specifying parcel-disjoint or geographically separated splits, spatial buffers, or patch overlap handling. Nearby pixels from the same fields could make classification easier and inflate apparent label efficiency. This is an uncertainty in the protocol, not evidence that leakage occurred.

The wildfire example does not substantiate claims of superior disturbance detection or temporal localization. Figure 5 presents UMAP visualizations for only two areas, without detection metrics or baseline comparisons; Appendix G mentions an RF evaluation but reports no results. More consequentially, the main text describes 2021 fires and embeddings, whereas Appendix G identifies the events as occurring in 2020. This unresolved mismatch undermines the interpretation that within-year fire timing is encoded.

The stocking-index experiment supports association more strongly than predictive generalization. All products are calibrated using the same 38 plots on which performance is reported, without held-out calibration assessment or uncertainty estimates. Moreover, TESSERA receives a locally trained GEDI regression model while alternatives are existing products. The claim that its advantage must arise from embedding efficiency is therefore not isolated by this comparison.

Several important implementation details are inconsistent or incomplete. Figure 1 specifies GRU pooling, whereas the text specifies attention pooling; Appendix A describes learnable additive temporal encodings, whereas the training description uses concatenated sine/cosine features. Projector depth also differs between descriptions. Quantization-aware training is insufficiently specified, and replacement sampling does not explain handling pixels with zero valid observations or an absent modality, despite the gap-free global claim.

The methodological contribution largely combines established temporal self-supervision, Barlow Twins, mixup, Transformers, and sensor fusion. The manuscript acknowledges the closely related temporal Barlow Twins approach of Lisaius et al., but does not directly isolate improvements over that approach. Ablations are confined to Austrian crops and do not test whether temporal order or day-of-year encoding is essential to the claimed temporal advantages.

Some broad performance and efficiency claims exceed the comparisons. BioMassters methods use different input processing and prediction heads, and downstream timing excludes TESSERA pretraining and embedding generation. These results demonstrate useful deployed pipelines but do not isolate architectural superiority or total computational savings. Nevertheless, the controlled canopy results, additional transfer evidence, and substantial resource contribution make the overall case favor acceptance.

strengths: The principal contribution is a useful representation system and data resource: annual, 10 m, 128-dimensional embeddings derived from optical and radar time series, with released weights, processing code, and a retrieval library. Precomputed embeddings substantially simplify downstream remote-sensing workflows. This practical contribution has value beyond architectural novelty.

The canopy-height experiment provides convincing evidence of representation quality. With identical U-Net heads and spatially disjoint training and testing regions, TESSERA achieves RMSE 8.88 ± 0.98 m versus 10.73 ± 1.10 m for PRESTO and 13.83 ± 0.32 m for GSE (Figure 3). Multiple spatial splits and training runs strengthen this comparison.

The quantitative evaluations cover classification, segmentation, and regression. Crop classification compares identical MLP heads across embeddings and includes scarce-label settings. BioMassters uses a fixed 2,773-patch test set and five random training splits; TESSERA with 1% of training labels outperforms SpectralGPT trained with the full dataset and approaches the supervised competition winner as labels increase.

The ablations provide useful engineering evidence. Removing global shuffling or mixup reduces crop validation F1 from 0.773 to 0.681 or 0.662, respectively, while removing quantization improves it only to 0.779 (Table 4). These results support the training pipeline and the storage-efficient representation.

Overall, the demonstrated transfer performance and potentially valuable open embedding resource support weak acceptance. The reservations below limit the breadth and attribution of the claims, but do not negate the strongest controlled results.
weaknesses: The crop evaluation does not adequately establish spatial independence. Appendix E describes random subsets and held-out validation/test sets without specifying parcel-level separation, geographic blocking, or prevention of overlap between segmentation patches. With strongly correlated pixels within agricultural fields, this leaves uncertainty about whether the reported gains and few-shot results reflect transfer to unseen fields or interpolation within familiar ones.

The wildfire study does not substantiate the claimed detection, timing, and severity capabilities quantitatively. Figure 5 presents UMAP visualizations for two regions without held-out prediction metrics or baseline comparisons; Appendix G mentions an RF evaluation but reports no results. More consequentially, the main text identifies 2021 fires and embeddings, whereas Appendix G identifies the named events as occurring in 2020. This ambiguity matters directly to the claim that embeddings capture within-year event timing.

Several comparisons cannot isolate the contribution of the learned representation. Locally trained canopy models are compared with unadapted global products, and BioMassters comparisons vary input preprocessing and decoder architecture. The manuscript acknowledges some differences, but its broad superiority claims exceed what these comparisons establish. The matched-head PRESTO/GSE comparisons are substantially stronger evidence.

The carbon-market experiment is an exploratory association study rather than a validated biomass predictor. All products are calibrated and evaluated against the same 38 plots, without held-out calibration or uncertainty estimates. Applying the same calibration to all products supports a descriptive comparison, but does not establish predictive generalization. The assertion that the improvement 'must' arise from embedding efficiency also overlooks differences in supervision, resolution, and regional adaptation.

Methodological novelty is primarily in integration and scale: temporal-subsampling Barlow Twins builds explicitly on prior work, and mixup is also borrowed. The ablations support these choices on one crop task, but do not establish their broader effects. Likewise, the scaling sweep on that task supports an empirical trend, rather than the stronger claim of predictable scaling laws.

Reproducibility is weakened by conflicting implementation descriptions: Figure 1 specifies GRU pooling while the text specifies attention pooling; temporal encoding is described both as learned additive embeddings and concatenated sine/cosine features; and projector depth differs between Appendices A and B. Quantization-aware training lacks implementation detail. These are correctable reporting issues, but concern substantive model choices. The global 'gap-free' claim also lacks an explanation for pixels with zero valid observations, which sampling with replacement cannot resolve.

strengths: TESSERA makes a useful contribution through global, annual, 10 m satellite representations that combine optical and radar time series. Precomputed 128-dimensional embeddings, released model weights and processing code, and the GEOTESSERA retrieval library substantially reduce the work required for downstream applications. This systems and resource contribution warrants recognition independently of architectural novelty.

The canopy-height experiment provides convincing evidence of representation quality: spatially held-out evaluation with matched U-Net heads and repeated runs yields RMSE of 8.88 ± 0.98 m, compared with 10.73 for PRESTO, 11.83 for GSE, and 11.60 for Sentinel-2 composites (Figure 3). These controlled comparisons are more persuasive than comparisons against existing global maps.

The quantitative experiments demonstrate useful transfer across classification and regression. Crop classification improves over PRESTO and GSE across label budgets, while BioMassters evaluation uses a fixed 2,773-patch test set and five random training splits. TESSERA with 1% of training labels outperforms SpectralGPT trained with the full dataset, and approaches the supervised competition winner with all labels.

The ablations support several practical design choices. Removing global shuffling or mixup reduces crop-validation F1 from 0.773 to 0.681 or 0.662, respectively; removing quantization improves it only to 0.779 (Table 4). This supports the storage–accuracy tradeoff central to distributing global embeddings. Overall, the demonstrated utility and substantial resource contribution favor acceptance despite the reservations below.
weaknesses: The crop evaluation does not adequately establish spatial independence. Appendix E describes randomly selected samples and held-out sets without specifying field-disjoint partitions or spatial separation; patch overlap handling is also unspecified. Correlated pixels from the same agricultural parcels could make performance, especially few-shot results, optimistic. The experiments support within-region prediction more clearly than generalization to unseen fields or regions.

The five-task superiority claim exceeds the evidence. Wildfire results mainly comprise UMAP visualizations from two regions, without reported quantitative detection results or baseline comparisons. Separation could reflect geography or land cover as well as fire timing. Moreover, Section 2.4 and Figure 5 describe 2021 fires and embeddings, whereas Appendix G identifies the events as occurring in 2020, materially obscuring the temporal-sensitivity claim.

The stocking-index experiment demonstrates association on a small sample rather than independently validated AGB prediction. All products are calibrated and evaluated on the same 38 plots, with no held-out calibration evaluation or uncertainty estimates. The claim that the advantage must arise from embedding efficiency is unsupported because target definitions, supervision, resolution, and processing also differ. Similarly, locally trained canopy models outperforming unadapted global products does not isolate representation quality.

Methodological novelty is primarily in integration and scale: temporal Barlow Twins representations and mixup are explicitly inherited from prior work. Ablations and scaling experiments use only Austrian crop classification, so they do not establish that the same design benefits transfer broadly. Biomass comparisons also change both input pipelines and decoder architectures, limiting attribution of improvements specifically to the representation.

Several implementation inconsistencies hinder reproducibility despite the extensive appendix: Figure 1 specifies GRU pooling while the text specifies attention pooling; temporal encoding is variously described as learned additive encoding and concatenated sine/cosine features; projector depth differs between Appendices A and B. Quantization and handling of completely missing modalities are insufficiently specified. The claimed gap-free, cloud-invariant coverage is therefore stronger than the documented handling of sparse observations.
